abstract: Threshold public goods games (TPGGs) are generally expected to facilitate coordination more effectively than linear public goods games (LPGGs), because an explicit provision point can support non-zero equilibria and transform a social dilemma into a coordination problem. This prediction, however, is based largely on settings in which group members contribute to a single shared pool. Whether it extends to environments in which individuals freely allocate resources across multiple partners remains unknown. Here, using a three-person ring network and functional near-infrared spectroscopy hyperscanning, we examined how free allocation shaped behavioral and neural signatures in the two game structures. Contrary to conventional expectations, the LPGG produced stronger partner-specific reciprocity and greater alignment to history-dependent contribution standards than the TPGG. This behavioral differentiation was accompanied by stronger dyadic inter-brain synchrony in the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex during the LPGG. The two structures also elicited distinct patterns of individual neural activity and dmPFC--rTPJ functional connectivity. These findings suggest that the expected coordination advantage of threshold public goods games may not generalize to settings that allow partner-specific resource allocation, highlighting the importance of allocation flexibility in shaping the relationship between game structure and cooperative behavior.
